slides.title: Converting Mass, Area and Volume
slides.note: Post the learning target. Say one line and nothing else yet: “Today: the same move on pounds and gallons — and for area, the length ratio is used twice.”

slides.title: Warm-Up
slides.note: Q4 is Notes II: a square foot is 12 by 12 inches, 144 of them, not 12. A room that writes 12 in² will write 36 for 3 ft². Q2 is yesterday's k² — the same structure. Two minutes silent, then reveal.

slides.title: Warm-Up
slides.note: Reveal. Ask for the band each question came from only if time allows.

slides.title: Vocabulary
slides.sub: The new words, before they are used.
slides.note: Read each word and its meaning once; the notes use them next. Students copy the words, not the definitions.

slides.title: Notes
slides.note: 1 lb = 0.454 kg is a form of 1 like 1 in = 2.54 cm. 50 lb × 0.454 = 22.7 kg, and the estimate says fewer kilograms than pounds (a kilogram is heavier). The sheet gives 1 kg = 2.204 lb for the way back. Volume the same: 1 gal = 3.785 L, so a 2-gal bucket is 7.57 L — more liters, since a liter is smaller. **Say:** a new quantity, the same move — the sheet's ratio, the estimate first.

slides.title: Notes
slides.note: 1 ft = 12 in, but a square foot is a 12 by 12 square: 144 in². Area is two lengths, so the ratio is used twice — 5.02–03's k² again, with 12 for k. 3 ft² = 3 × 144 = 432 in². The grid shows it: 12 rows of 12. Across systems the same: 1 ft = 0.305 m, so a square foot is 0.305 × 0.305 = 0.093 m² — the sheet's length ratio, squared, is the only area ratio there is. **Say:** square units, square the ratio.

slides.title: Notes
slides.note: The sheet has 1 c = 8 fl oz and 1 c = 0.24 L, and no line from fluid ounces to milliliters — so a fluid ounce reaches liters through cups: a 12-fl-oz can is 12 ÷ 8 = 1.5 c, and 1.5 × 0.24 = 0.36 L. Two forms of 1 in a chain, like yesterday's yards. And a fluid ounce is a volume; the ounce on a scale is a weight — two units that share a word. **Say:** read the sheet for the path; it is never one guessed number.

slides.title: Example 1
slides.note: Ask which is heavier, a pound or a kilogram, before anyone multiplies.

slides.title: Example 1
slides.note: 31.78 kg. Fewer kilograms than pounds. A board with 154.28 multiplied by 2.204, the other ratio — the inverted-ratio error again. (70 ÷ 2.204 = 31.76 is the sheet's other route; accept it.)

slides.title: Your Turn
slides.sub: Same steps, your numbers. Boards up when done.
slides.note: 40.86 kg — 40.9 to one place. A board with 198.36 used 2.204.

slides.title: Your Turn
slides.note: Reveal; name what a wrong board most likely did (see the note above).

slides.title: Example 2
slides.note: Ask how many times the ratio is used before anyone multiplies.

slides.title: Example 2
slides.note: 720 in². The ratio twice: 12² = 144 per square foot. A board with 60 used it once — the lesson's named error.

slides.title: Your Turn
slides.sub: Same steps, your numbers. Boards up when done.
slides.note: 45 ft². 3² = 9 per square yard. A board with 15 used 3 once. (Board 6 asks the metric square unit as a vote — nothing on this slide gives it away.)

slides.title: Your Turn
slides.note: Reveal; name what a wrong board most likely did (see the note above).

slides.title: Whiteboards   ·   Question 1 of 9
slides.note: Kilograms to pounds — more pounds, as the estimate says. (10 ÷ 0.454 = 22.03 by the other sheet ratio; accept it.)

slides.title: Whiteboards   ·   Question 4 of 9
slides.note: Diagnostic. D is the lesson's named error — the ratio once on a square unit — and the 3 by 3 grid of square feet inside a square yard is the picture that answers it. Sixty seconds and a re-vote on a split.

slides.title: Whiteboards   ·   Question 4 of 9
slides.note: Reveal. Scan the back row first; question the blank boards before the wrong ones.

slides.title: Whiteboards   ·   Question 5 of 9
slides.note: Fluid ounces go through cups — the sheet has no fl-oz-to-milliliter line. A board with 3.84 multiplied 16 by 0.24, treating fluid ounces as cups.

slides.title: Whiteboards   ·   Question 5 of 9

slides.title: Whiteboards   ·   Question 6 of 9
slides.note: The boundary board: the familiar 100 is wrong. D is the whole lesson's trap in one vote — the metric 100 feels like it should survive squaring, and it does not. On a split, draw the 100 by 100 square.

slides.title: Whiteboards   ·   Question 6 of 9

slides.title: Whiteboards   ·   Question 7 of 9
slides.note: Two units, one question: nothing compares until the units match. A board that said 'the flour, because 5 > 2.5' compared the numbers and not the weights — and it is wrong. (5 × 0.454 = 2.27 kg against 2.5 kg, by the other route: the sugar, by 0.23 kg.)

slides.title: Whiteboards   ·   Question 8 of 9
slides.note: The extra-number board (ruling 22): the price is bait. A board with 170.33 multiplied the price by 3.785 — a number that was never asked for.

slides.title: Whiteboards   ·   Question 8 of 9

slides.title: Whiteboards   ·   Question 9 of 9
slides.sub: Take your time. Boards up when you have written it.
slides.note: Written, and the exit evidence: the area rule pushed one step further, by the room, with no example of a cube shown first. 'Twice' is a board that remembered today's rule and not its reason — three lengths, three ratios.

slides.title: Independent Set
slides.sub: Six questions. On your own, in writing.
slides.note: Hand out the Independent Set; the same six questions are on the board. Silent work. Circulate and mark what you see; do not teach. Whatever is not finished goes home.
